items.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: I had heard the Thad Jones and Mel Lewis things and I’d heard some Basie and Ellington and Kenton, Maynard Ferguson’s early 60s stuff, Woody Herman.

ctx.x: sounded as modern as anything anybody was doing, but first of all they always sounded like jazz because they had the jazz beat. And then they also sounded like jazz because they also had this incredible mixture of the chromatic tonal harmony that you hear in European music from around the time of Bach through at least the Russian composers who still had ties with tonality whether it was in an obvious way like with Rachmaninoff or a less obvious way like with Shostakovich and Prokofiev or early Stravinsky, there…

Lee Lewis, Little Richard and that kind of stuff. And he had an upright piano in the house. That’s another thing that I read that’s an interesting, worthwhile point too that at the turn of the twentieth century the biggest disseminator of music in America was the piano. So that shows you, you know, people today just push a button and it all just happens for them. We’d get back to his place and sometimes he could actually sit down and play the chorus of the rhythm & blues or boogie woogie piano from his Jerry Lee…

it was I guess one of the things that threw me off. Because the melody is real simple too. It’s a B flat blues and has lots of minor thirds [plays piano], then it goes to the four [plays piano], and then to one [plays piano] and then to five [plays piano] and then one again before it hits the tonic, which has the fifth in the melody or no, the third in the melody [plays piano].
